product.olivetti-pcs42p-s2-50-e.summary: The move to a doubled clock among the PCS42P Entry models, in a large case with more expansion space.
product.olivetti-pcs42p-s2-50-e.history: The PCS42P S2/50 E belonged to the PCS range for personal use, study and entertainment, as described in MCmicrocomputer 137 (February 1994, p. 176). Olivetti included it in the same modular line as the M4-4xx, with the Entry platform and large TIN BOX case; the PCS42P S2/50 offered the other case. A Gladrags review (February 1996), preserved as a reproduction, shows a PCS42P with educational software and games without identifying its CPU variant. Identity sources: Pocket Service Guide, pp. 4-1–3.
product.olivetti-pcs42p-s2-50-e.warning: Historical research sheet; no creation profile or validation of this commercial model in BluMach.
product.olivetti-pcs42p-s2-50-e.technica: The case and board distinguish this configuration from its siblings. The manual identifies PCS42P S2/50 E as XST41 S50, with a Entry board, a 50 MHz CPU and a 25 MHz bus. In its table, S identifies the compact M4 case and E the large PCS42P case; E does not mean Entry.

RAM expands through two modules. The guide supports 4–64 MB in two 70 ns SIMM banks: 4/8/16/32 MB modules with parity or 4/8 MB without parity, including mixed populations. It provides for 128 or 256 KB L2 cache; standard installation is not assumed.

Case size determines how many cards fit. The IN2024 riser offers 5 positions: two shared ISA/VESA and 3 ISA; the motherboard also provides an AT connection for audio. The guide specifies a 200 W power supply (pp. 4-2–3).

The BIOS can be updated from floppy disk. The manual lists revisions 1.09–1.11 and calls the 28F001BX ‘1 MB’ (pp. 4-7 and 4-10); Intel specifies 1 Mbit, 128K × 8, or 128 KiB (290406-007, p. 1). These are different units; retaining the manual’s wording does not endorse that capacity.

A dump attributed to BA2142 enables firmware research for the Entry family. Static observation: 128 KiB and ‘Resident Diagnostics Ver. 1.11’ at offset 0x8132. Its hash is verified; the donor, commercial model and identity with the manual’s BIOS 1.11 remain unconfirmed.

The manual’s configurations have been cross-checked and preserved files verified. BluMach includes the experimental olivetti_ba2142 board targeting Entry; this does not validate the 26 commercial configurations or establish equivalence with Enhanced.

This model cannot yet be created from the sheet. Its board and ROM set need identification, followed by validation of boot, RAM, video, keyboard, CMOS, disks and resets. The BA2142 baseline uses a chipset approximation and read-only Flash; its code also disagrees between a UMC label and an OPTi device. No dump execution test or new antivirus scan has been performed.
Olivetti, Personal Computer — Pocket Service Guide, M4-4x4/M4-4x2/PCS42P chapter, pp. 4-1–7, 4-10 and 4-13: identity, architecture and revisions; discrepancies retained.
Paolo Ciardelli, ‘Olivetti M4-62 Modulo’, MCmicrocomputer 137, February 1994, p. 176: positioning of the M4, PCS and M6 ranges; the M4-62 price is not transferred.
Intel, 1-Mbit Boot Block Flash Memory, 290406-007, November 1995, p. 1: 28F001BX capacity; the date belongs to the document, not the computer.
BluMach 88f74ba3, machine_table.c and m_at_socket1.c: experimental BA2142 platform, code comparison without validation of this model.

Entry integrates video and disk control to leave expansion slots free. The guide specifies CL-GD5424 with 512 KB expandable to 1 MB and SMC37C651 for floppy and IDE. BA2142 derives from BA2148 Entry; that revision is not assigned to every unit. The 82C611 belongs to Enhanced (pp. 4-3 and 4-7).
Gladrags, February 1996, PCS42P clipping reproduced by Soumyadip Choudhury in Cutting the Chai (2008). No CPU identified; its 74,195-rupee price is not assigned to this variant.
